3.3.3.1-f1.text: Foecundam & multiplicem perniciem, fontem cladium & seminarium delictorum

translations.literal: A fruitful and manifold destruction, a fountain of slaughters and a seed-plot of crimes
translations.note: Cyprian uses this language of envy and jealousy (zelus), almost certainly in his treatise De zelo et livore; Burton gives no title. Cladium means 'disasters' or 'slaughters', which Burton renders freely as 'murders'.

3.3.3.1-f2.text: Phaerus Aegypti rex de caecitate oraculum consulens, visum ei rediturum accepit, si oculos abluisset lotio mulieris, quae aliorum virorum esset expers, uxoris urinam expertus nihil profecit & aliarum frustra, eas omnes (ea excepta per quam curatus fuit) unum in locum coactas concremavit

translations.literal: Pheros king of Egypt, consulting the oracle about blindness, received that sight would return to him if he had washed his eyes with the urine of a woman who was without share of other men; having tried his wife's urine he profited nothing, and of others in vain; all of them (that one excepted by whom he was cured), driven together into one place, he burned up.
translations.note: Burton summarises the story in his own Latin; it is not a quotation of Herodotus' wording. In Herodotus the king then married the woman whose urine cured him. The parenthesis is in the source.
translations.text: Pheros, king of Egypt, consulted the oracle about his blindness and was told that his sight would return if he washed his eyes with the urine of a woman who had had nothing to do with any man but her husband. He tried his wife's urine and got no benefit, and other women's in vain; so he gathered them all into one place, except the one by whom he was cured, and burned them.

translations.literal: on account of suspicion of concubinage
translations.note: pellicatus means keeping a concubine, or adultery with one. In Cicero the wife is named Thebe.
translations.text: on suspicion that he kept a mistress
